entries.title: Types and conversions
entries.summary: Integer and floating types, how values are converted, integer division.
entries.syntax: int8_t … int64_t, uint8_t … uint64_t, size_t, float, double, char, void
entries.description:
Prefer the fixed-width types of <stdint.h> when the size matters. `char` is meant for text; for a raw byte use `uint8_t`. `size_t` is the unsigned type of `sizeof` results and of most sizes and counts in the library (print it with `%zu`).
Conversions: in an expression the narrower operand is promoted to the wider type; in an assignment the right-hand value is converted to the type of the variable (floating → integer truncates toward zero). A cast `(type) expr` forces a conversion.

details.name: Integer division
details.text: `7 / 2` is 3 and `-7 / 2` is -3 (truncation toward zero). `%` gives the remainder: `7 % 2` is 1.

details.name: Mixed arithmetic
details.text: `7 / 2.0` is 3.5 because one operand is double. `(double) a / b` converts before dividing; `(double)(a / b)` converts after.

details.name: Float literals
details.text: `3.14` is a double; `3.14f` is a float.

mistakes: Dividing two ints and expecting a fraction.
Assuming `int` or `long` has a given size: use <stdint.h> types when it matters.

entries.title: Operators and precedence
entries.summary: All the operators of the course, from highest to lowest precedence.
entries.description: From highest to lowest: `()` `[]` `.` `->`; unary `! ~ ++ -- + - * & sizeof (cast)` (right to left); `* / %`; `+ -`; `<< >>`; `< <= > >=`; `== !=`; `&`; `^`; `|`; `&&`; `||`; `?:`; assignments `= += -= …` (right to left); `,`. When in doubt, add parentheses.

details.name: Logical
details.text: `&&` `||` `!` yield 0 or 1. `&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right side is evaluated only if needed (`p != NULL && p->x > 0` is safe).

details.name: Increment
details.text: `i++` yields the old value then increments; `++i` increments then yields the new value.

details.name: Bitwise
details.text: `& | ^ ~` act on each bit; `<< >>` shift. `x << n` multiplies by 2^n for small non-negative values.

details.name: Assignment
details.text: `a += b` means `a = a + b`. `=` is assignment, `==` is comparison.

entries.example:
if (x = 5) { }        /* BUG: assigns 5 (always true); you meant == */
int a = 3, b = a++;   /* b == 3, a == 4 */
mistakes: Writing `=` instead of `==` in a condition (compile with -Wall to be warned).
Modifying the same variable twice in one expression (`i = i++ + 1`): undefined.

entries.title: Control flow
entries.summary: if/else, switch, while, do-while and for.
entries.description: Conditions are integers: 0 is false, anything else true. `switch` works only on integer values; each `case` falls through to the next one unless it ends with `break`. `do … while` runs its body at least once. In `for`, the three parts are optional.

details.name: break / continue
details.text: `break` leaves the innermost loop or switch; `continue` jumps to the next iteration.

details.name: switch fall-through
details.text: Deliberate fall-through is legal but easy to get wrong; gcc -Wextra warns about it.

entries.example:
for (int i = 0; i < argc; i++)
    printf("%s\n", argv[i]);
mistakes: A stray `;` after `if (…)` or `for (…)` makes the body empty.

entries.title: static
entries.summary: Static local variables keep their value; static globals and functions are private to the file.
entries.description: Inside a function, a `static` variable is created once, initialised once (with a constant) and keeps its value between calls. At file level, `static` limits the name's visibility to that source file (internal linkage), which is how modules hide helpers.
mistakes: Expecting a static local to be re-initialised on every call.

entries.title: sizeof
entries.summary: Size in bytes of a type or an object, as a size_t.
entries.description: Computed at compile time. On an array variable it is the size of the whole array; on a pointer it is the size of an address (4 or 8 bytes), not of what it points to. When an array is passed to a function it becomes a pointer, so `sizeof` inside the function gives the pointer size.
mistakes: Using sizeof on a pointer parameter to find the number of elements.

entries.title: Preprocessor
entries.description: The preprocessor works on text before the compiler. `<…>` searches the system directories, `"…"` searches the current directory first. Macros are plain text substitution: parenthesise the parameters and the whole expansion. A header should protect itself against double inclusion with `#pragma once` or an `#ifndef` guard.
entries.example:
#define MAX_SIZE 64
#define SQR(x) ((x) * (x))
int v[MAX_SIZE];
int s = SQR(2 + 1);   /* 9, because of the parentheses */
mistakes: `#define SQR(x) x * x` makes `SQR(2 + 1)` expand to `2 + 1 * 2 + 1`.
A `;` at the end of a `#define` becomes part of every expansion.

entries.title: Functions and arguments
entries.summary: Prototypes, pass by value, passing addresses, arrays as parameters.
entries.syntax:
type name(type a, type b);   /* prototype */
type name(type a, type b) { … return value; }
entries.description: A function must be declared (at least by a prototype) before it is called. Arguments are always passed BY VALUE: the function works on copies. To let a function modify the caller's variable, pass its address and write through the pointer. An array argument is passed as a pointer to its first element, so the size must be passed separately.
mistakes: Writing `swap(int a, int b)` and expecting the caller's variables to change.
Returning the address of a local variable: it no longer exists after the function returns.

entries.title: main, argc, argv, envp
entries.syntax:
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
int main(int argc, char *argv[], char *envp[])
entries.description: `argc` is the number of arguments including the program name; `argv[0]` is the program name, `argv[1]` … `argv[argc-1]` the arguments, and `argv[argc]` is NULL. Every argument is a string: use `atoi`/`strtol` to get numbers. `envp` (a common Unix extension) is a NULL-terminated array of `"NAME=value"` strings; `getenv` is the portable way to read one variable. The return value of `main` is the exit status (0 = success).
mistakes: Starting the loop at 0 and treating the program name as an argument.
